body_ar: ثم قال: باب الصفات عقد هذا الباب لصفات الحروف، والصفة في الأصل النعت وما يميز الشيء عن غيره، والصفات ثلاثة أقسام في الأصل، صفات ذاتية، وصفات عرضية، وصفات حكمية، فالصفات الذاتية هي ما خلق الله عليه الشيء كطول الإنسان وقصره وحسنه وقبحه وبياضه وسواده ونحو ذلك هذه صفة ذاتية فيه، والصفات العرضية كالصفات الاختيارية أو الفعلية كالحركة والسكون في الإنسان، والكلام والسكوت، هذا صفة عرضية أي تعرض للإنسان، والقسم الثالث الصفات الحكمية وهي: ما ناطه الشارع به من الأحكام، كالطهارة والنجاسة، كون هذا الشيء طاهرا وكونه نجسا هذا ليس من خلقته، ولا هو عارض فيه بل هو حكم رتبه الشارع عليه، وهذا عند جمهور أهل العلم خلافا للحنفية فالحنفية يرون أن الصفات الحكمية من الصفات الأصلية لا من الصفات العارضة، فيجعلون الأحكام أصولا يرون أن الشارع كاشف لما كان سابقا في أصل الخلقة، فيرون أن الأصل في الماء الطهارة فهو صفة أصلية له، وأن الأصل في البول النجاسة فهو صفة أصلية له،
body_en:
Then he said: "Chapter on the qualities." He set up this chapter for the qualities of the letters. A quality (ṣifah), in origin, is a descriptive attribute, and whatever distinguishes a thing from something else. Qualities are, in origin, of three kinds: essential qualities, accidental qualities, and juridically assigned qualities.

The essential qualities are those upon which God created the thing — such as a person's tallness or shortness, his beauty or ugliness, his whiteness or blackness, and the like; this is an essential quality in him.

The accidental qualities are such as the volitional or active qualities — like motion and rest in a person, and speech and silence; this is an accidental quality, that is, one that comes upon the person.

The third kind is the juridically assigned qualities, and they are the rulings that the Lawgiver has attached to the thing — such as ritual purity (ṭahārah) and substantive impurity (najāsah). That this thing is pure, and that it is impure, is not part of how it was created, nor is it something accidental in it; rather it is a ruling that the Lawgiver has ordered upon it. This is so in the view of the majority of the people of knowledge, as against the Hanafis: for the Hanafis hold that the juridically assigned qualities are among the original qualities and not among the accidental ones. So they make the rulings foundational, holding that the Lawgiver is disclosing what was already there in the original constitution of the thing; and thus they hold that the original state of water is purity, so that this is an original quality of it, and that the original state of urine is impurity, so that this is an original quality of it,

The published page carries only the opening excerpt of this tape; the Arabic breaks off and the full text is offered on the site as a downloadable Word document. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends. Nothing has been supplied to complete it.

The position attributed to the Hanafis here is reported, not adopted. The Sheikh states the majority view first and marks the Hanafi view as against it. The attribution must stay visible in any rendering.

The terms 'essential' (dhātiyyah) and 'accidental' (ʿaraḍiyyah) qualities are used here of created things and of letters. They are not being used in their creedal (kalām) sense, of the attributes of God, and the creedal senses must not be read into this passage.

The Arabic breaks off mid-sentence while still reporting the Hanafi position, before the Sheikh returns to his own voice or to the qualities of the letters that the chapter is about. A reader could mistake the last-stated position for his own; it is not.

al-Jazariyyah is the versified primer on Qur'anic recitation by Ibn al-Jazari, and 'the author' throughout this series is Ibn al-Jazari. The series title is left transliterated and untranslated. Articles 436-446 are tapes of this one series; their tape numbering in the titles does not run in the same order as the article IDs.
